title: Carbon farming

definition.text: A set of farming and forestry methods meant to store carbon from the air in soil and living plant material.

facts.text: Its overall goal is a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere, by speeding up how fast carbon is locked into soil and plants.
Converting forests, grasslands or savannas into cropland cuts the soil's organic carbon by about 30–40%.
Methods include changing tillage and grazing, using mulch or compost, adding biochar, and changing which crops are grown.
Mixing biochar into soil locks away roughly 50% of the carbon in the original biomass.
Carbon farming could offset as much as 20% of 2010 carbon dioxide emissions each year; by 2016 its variants covered hundreds of millions of hectares.
The stored carbon is not permanent: disturbing the soil or tilling intensively turns it back into a net source of greenhouse gases.
If incentives reward only stored carbon, it could encourage land clearing, monocultures and biodiversity loss.
Farmers who store carbon can sell carbon credits to companies that need offsets, as in Australia.

contested_note: Sources say the effect of more soil carbon on crop yield is unsettled, and critics doubt the practices can spread widely enough to matter.

definition.text: Growing bamboo plantations as a way to store carbon on farmland.

facts.text: A bamboo forest holds less total carbon than most mature forests but can match rubber plantations and orchards and exceed agroforests, palm oil plantations and grasslands.
Bamboo plantations take up carbon faster than mature forests, but only when new or actively managed.

title: 4 per 1000 initiative

definition.text: A France-led international effort to raise the carbon in farm and forest soils by 0.4% a year.

facts.text: It is the largest international effort to promote carbon farming.

notes: No page of its own; only the Carbon farming page mentions it. Keep only if it passes a curriculum test at selection.

title: Climate-smart agriculture

definition.text: A set of farming methods that try at once to adapt farming to climate change, raise yields for food security, and cut farm greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: The World Bank calls it practices and technologies that together boost productivity, build resilience and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
The FAO says it is not a new set of practices but an approach fitted to local contexts.
Examples include heat-tolerant crop varieties, mulching, boundary trees and suitable housing and spacing for cattle.
Carbon farming is one of its components.
Agriculture, forestry and land use produce 13%–21% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Rainfed farming makes up 80% of global agriculture, so shifting rainfall threatens many poor farmers in Asia and Africa.
No accepted standard defines it, and critics call the label greenwashing for big businesses.

contested_note: Critics argue the label has no standard and can be used to greenwash.

definition.text: Designing climate-smart farming programmes to address the different constraints and abilities of women and men farmers.

facts.text: Women farmers in developing countries face more climate risk because they have less access to land resources, money and advice.
They are often left out of decisions, which can limit their adoption of practices that help them adapt.

definition.text: A scoring tool that measures how resilient farming systems are to climate change.

facts.text: The global version benchmarks countries with nine indicators in three dimensions: productivity and resource efficiency, environmental sustainability and climate impact, and socio-economic resilience.
It sorts nations into four levels, from Highly Resilient to Very Low Resilience.
A version for India uses 26 indicators to compare the country's agro-climatic zones.

definition.text: The heat-trapping gases released by farming, both directly from crops and livestock and indirectly from clearing land for farms.

facts.text: Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute 13%–21% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Nitrous oxide and methane make up over half of agriculture's direct emissions.
Making and using nitrogen fertilizer contributes around 5% of all global greenhouse gas emissions.
Livestock production alone accounts for almost 60% of food-system greenhouse gas emissions.
Ruminants such as cows and sheep give off methane made by microbes in their guts.
